findings.finding: FTC v. Epic Games (Fortnite): $245M in refunds for unwanted charges, finalized March 2023 (4-0 vote), separate from a $275M COPPA penalty. Allegations: confusing/inconsistent button layout let a single press trigger a purchase; children could buy currency without parental involvement; accounts were locked when players disputed charges with their card company. Order bars charging via dark patterns or without affirmative consent, and bars blocking account access over disputed charges. Refund rounds: over $72M sent Dec 2024, over $126M sent June 2025; over 37M people were notified.
findings.applyHow: Every spend (real money AND gems) needs a two-step confirm: tap item, then a separate confirm screen showing what is bought and the cost. No one-tap buy, no purchase button adjacent to play/preview/close buttons, no purchase on wake/loading. Add an easy undo/refund for unused gem-bought items (e.g. a short self-serve refund window if the item is unused). Never lock or punish an account because a card dispute was filed: only claw back the disputed gems/items, keep everything else accessible.

findings.finding: US v. Cognosphere (HoYoverse, Genshin Impact), announced Jan 17 2025: $20M penalty. Proposed order bans selling loot boxes to under-16s without parental consent, bans selling loot boxes via virtual currency without an option to buy directly in US dollars, requires disclosure of loot box odds and real-money cost, and COPPA compliance. Complaint alleged bundled, multi-tier virtual currency obscured real cost for children and teens. Commissioner Ferguson concurred only on COPPA and odds-deception counts and dissented on the rest, so the currency-obfuscation theory is not settled FTC doctrine. FTC business blog repeats: avoid dark patterns, be truthful about cost.
findings.applyHow: Keep the no-loot-box promise absolute: no paid randomized rewards of any kind (no mystery crates, spin wheels, blind bags bought with gems or with bones that gems can buy). One premium currency only (gems), no gem-to-second-currency chain. Show the dollar price next to every gem price (e.g. '300 gems, about $2.99'), computed from the smallest/base pack rate with no bulk discount. Where practical, offer the bigger items for direct dollar purchase as well as gems.

findings.finding: Whether the Cognosphere order was entered by the court: FTC pages describe it as proposed and needing a federal judge's approval (C.D. Cal. case 2:25-cv-00447). One secondary outlet says the FTC 'finalized' the $20M settlement; I could not confirm the entry date from a primary source. I found no FTC game-specific in-app purchase/loot box action dated 2026; 2025-2026 COPPA activity found was Apitor (Sept 2025, third-party SDK collecting kids' geolocation) and Illuminate Education (June 2026, not a game).
findings.applyHow: Treat the Genshin order terms as the working standard regardless of entry status. The Apitor case means any third-party script in the game (Stripe.js, fonts, CDN, embedded merch iframe) is the developer's COPPA responsibility: load Stripe and the merch shop only behind the grown-up gate, not on the play screen.

findings.finding: Amended COPPA Rule: FTC approved Jan 16 2025 (5-0), published in Federal Register April 22 2025, effective June 23 2025, general compliance deadline April 22 2026 (already passed). Key changes: separate opt-in verifiable parental consent before disclosing children's data to third parties (incl. targeted ads), data kept only as long as needed (no indefinite retention), personal information now includes biometric and government identifiers, safe harbor transparency. Proposed push-notification limits were dropped. On Feb 25 2026 the FTC issued a policy statement that it will not bring COPPA actions for collecting data solely to verify age in certain circumstances.
findings.applyHow: Keep the no-analytics/no-tracking promise as the compliance strategy: collect nothing from the player. Save progress locally or under a random ID with no email. Write a short data-retention line in the privacy policy (purchase records kept for tax/refund purposes only, held by the grown-up's Stripe record, not tied to a child profile).

findings.finding: COPPA applies to under-13s. A service is covered if 'directed to children' (multi-factor test: subject matter, visual content, animated characters, child-oriented activities, age of models, etc.; no single factor decides; FTC notes some animated characters are general-audience) or if a general-audience operator has actual knowledge it collects personal information from a child. A 'mixed audience' service (children not the primary audience) may use a neutral age screen but must not collect personal info before screening and may not block children altogether. Persistent identifiers are personal information, but need no notice/consent when used only for 'support for internal operations' (maintaining functioning, authentication, personalization such as game scores/character choices; not behavioral advertising) and no other personal info is collected. A card used in connection with a monetary transaction is a listed parental-consent method (with notice of each transaction to the account holder); a card number alone is not.
findings.applyHow: A cartoon-style dog game that the developer knows children play should be designed as mixed-audience/child-directed, not argued to be general-audience. Rules: no account, email, name, chat, photo upload or free-text fields on the child side; only a random save ID. All data entry (email for receipt, shipping address for merch, card) happens inside Stripe Checkout or the merch site, reached only through the grown-up gate. The grown-up gate is a purchase safeguard, not COPPA consent, so do not rely on it to justify collecting child data. Stripe emailing a receipt per transaction to the cardholder matches the 'notice of each discrete transaction' element.

findings.finding: FTC 'click-to-cancel' (amended Negative Option Rule) was vacated by the Eighth Circuit on July 8 2025 for skipping a required preliminary regulatory analysis. The FTC restarted rulemaking: draft ANPRM to OIRA Jan 30 2026, ANPRM published March 13 2026 (docket FTC-2026-0265), comments closed April 13 2026. As of the latest sources found (to about May 2026) no proposed or final rule exists; I could not confirm any later step. Enforcement continues under ROSCA and FTC Act Section 5; the ANPRM lists the working principles: disclose material terms, clearly and conspicuously, before consent, get express informed consent, honor a simple cancellation.
findings.applyHow: If a subscription is added (e.g. a monthly supporter pass with a gem stipend): state price, billing interval and 'renews until cancelled' right beside the buy button before Checkout; no pre-ticked boxes; cancel online in the same place it was bought, in two clicks, via Stripe customer portal link in every receipt; no free-trial-to-paid conversion for a kids-adjacent game. Simplest safe option: sell one-time passes (e.g. a 30-day pass that just expires) instead of auto-renewal.

findings.finding: California's Automatic Renewal Law amendments (AB 2863) apply to contracts entered, amended or extended on or after July 1 2025: express affirmative consent to the auto-renewal terms, records of that consent retained, free-trial conversions covered, annual reminder for subscriptions sent via the same medium used to sign up, cancellation in the same medium the consumer used to subscribe, and no misrepresentation of material terms. Commentators note many vacated federal click-to-cancel requirements live on in new or enhanced state auto-renewal laws. Summary is from law-firm alerts, not the statute text; other states' specifics were not individually checked.
findings.applyHow: Build any subscription to the California standard for all US buyers: separate consent checkbox for the renewal terms (logged with timestamp on the server), confirmation email with terms and cancel link, pre-renewal reminder email (Stripe can send renewal reminders), online cancel that takes effect immediately with no retention maze. Avoid annual plans at launch to skip the annual-notice machinery.

findings.finding: EU CPC Network 'Key Principles on In-game Virtual Currencies', published 21 March 2025 (non-binding, but states authorities' reading of existing law; applies to currencies bought with real money, excludes currency obtainable only through gameplay). Seven principles: (1) price in real-world money must be clearly and prominently displayed for both the currency and each item, calculated at full price without quantity discounts; (2) avoid obscuring cost: do not mix multiple paid currencies or require several exchanges; (3) do not force unwanted currency purchases: no bundles mismatched to item prices, let consumers choose the specific amount; (4) give pre-contractual information (trader identity and contact, main characteristics, real price, withdrawal right, payment/delivery); (5) respect the 14-day right of withdrawal, including for unused purchased currency; digital content is exempt only with express consent plus acknowledgment given separately from the buy click; (6) fair, plain-language terms: no unilateral right to change currency value, remove purchased content, or ban accounts without a way to contest; (7) respect vulnerabilities: any game not exclusively for adults should expect many under-18 players; do not directly exhort children to buy or to persuade adults to buy; provide parental controls with real-money spending disabled by default; do not build the model on 'whales'. Same day the CPC opened an action against Star Stable Online (time-limited offers pressuring children, unclear pricing). The Commission later said industry dialogue was unsatisfactory and nine companies have been targeted in coordinated actions.
findings.applyHow: Design to this once and it covers the US too. Gem packs priced so the smallest pack buys the cheapest paid item exactly (no leftover-gem trap); ideally a 'buy exactly what I need' option at checkout (top up the shortfall). Dollar price shown on every gem-priced item. Spending off by default until a grown-up unlocks the shop. No 'ask your grown-up to buy this!' prompts, no begging dog animation tied to a purchase. Terms: gems never expire, prices in gems are not raised on already-owned gems, purchased items are permanent. For EU/UK buyers add a separate 'deliver now, I understand I lose the 14-day withdrawal right' tick box and still refund unused gems within 14 days.

findings.finding: European Commission proposal for a Digital Fairness Act, COM(2026) 1100 final, dated 11 Nov 2026 (proposal only; would apply 12 months after entry into force, after Parliament and Council adopt it). Would repeal the UCPD and, per the explanatory text: Art. 14 requires the real-world monetary value of items priced in paid-for virtual currency to be shown prominently (estimated at full price without quantity discounts); recital 62 says that where a product is directed at minors (under 18) or the trader knows with reasonable certainty minors use it, virtual currencies should be disabled by default and activated only with parent/guardian approval; Art. 15 requires probability disclosure for variable reward systems, bans paid ones for minors and requires an off switch for everyone; Art. 16 bans pay-to-win and pay-to-progress mechanisms for minors; Art. 17 off-switch for addictive features; Arts. 20-27 require reminders before free-trial conversion and auto-renewal and an easy cancellation facility; drip pricing prohibited. An age rating indicating suitability for under-18s counts as 'directed at minors'.
findings.applyHow: This is the direction of travel and it hits exactly this game's profile. Structure new spend so it is future-proof: paid items should be cosmetic, convenience-free extras, expansions or supporter perks, never a paywall on mission progress or a paid speed-up that makes the free path feel broken (no pay-to-progress energy timers, no paid skip of grind that was tuned to hurt). Keep gems locked until a grown-up enables them, per device. Final text may change; re-check before any EU marketing push.

findings.finding: UK: no loot box legislation; industry self-regulation via Ukie's 11 principles on paid loot boxes (18 July 2023, 12-month implementation to July 2024), covering loot boxes bought with money or with purchased currency. Government said in January 2026 that legislative options remain under review (secondary source). CAP/ASA 'Guidance on advertising in-game purchases': if virtual currency can only be obtained by purchase, the in-game storefront counts as advertising under the CAP Code; if it can also be earned in-game the storefront is generally outside remit (but app store listings are always in remit). Item value must be clear, bundles with varying price-per-unit are a flagged risk, ads must not imply paying is the only route when a free route exists, and ads must not directly exhort children to buy. ASA enforcement notice on loot box disclosure in app store listings: active monitoring from 26 May 2026; 'Offers In-App Purchases' alone is not enough if loot boxes exist.
findings.applyHow: On the landing page and any store listing state plainly: 'Optional in-game purchases. No random paid items. No ads.' Shop copy for kids' eyes is descriptive only ('Trail hat, 200 gems, about $1.99'), never imperative ('Buy now!', 'Don't miss out!'). If an item can also be earned with bones, say so on the same card.

findings.finding: I could not find a primary CMA source for 2025-2026 guidance specific to in-game purchases or virtual currency under the DMCC Act. General DMCC drip-pricing and unfair-practice rules exist but were not verified here.
findings.applyHow: Show the full all-in price before Checkout (pack price plus any tax line shown by Stripe); no fees added at the last step. Have UK-specific advice checked before targeting UK buyers.

findings.finding: Stripe Tax: monitors Stripe-processed sales per state against economic nexus thresholds and alerts by email/Dashboard, but 'it's up to you to confirm whether registration is actually required'; it does not monitor the home state; alerts start once the account has $10,000 revenue in the previous year. It only calculates/collects tax in states where a registration has been added. Stripe can register on the seller's behalf and file US returns (Tax Complete tiers from $90/month on a 1-year contract). Pay-as-you-go pricing: 0.5% of volume for Checkout/no-code integrations, charged only in jurisdictions where registered (50 cents per transaction via API). Typical thresholds per Stripe guides: $100,000 in sales in most states, sometimes paired with 200 transactions; $500,000 in California, New York and Texas; $250,000 in Alabama. Washington: $100,000 gross sales, previous or current calendar year. Digital goods taxability varies by state. Some states (Stripe names Arizona, Indiana, North Carolina) count non-taxable sales toward thresholds.
findings.applyHow: Turn on Stripe Tax monitoring now (free until registered), set a digital-goods product tax code on gem packs and passes, and collect billing postal code/state in Checkout so sales are attributed (country-only US sales go 'unattributed' and are not monitored). Below roughly $100k/year into any one state there is normally no out-of-state collection duty; register only when Stripe flags a state. Budget 0.5% of sales in registered states. Thresholds change; confirm with a tax professional before registering.

findings.finding: Oregon has no general state or local sales/use tax (Oregon DOR; Stripe's Oregon page: 'N/A, no state sales tax registration to add'). Stripe notes an Oregon-based business can still owe sales tax on sales to customers in other states, and Oregon imposes other business taxes such as income tax.
findings.applyHow: No sales tax on sales to Oregon players. Do not advertise 'tax-free' game-wide: buyers in other states may be charged once the developer is registered there. Let Stripe Checkout display any tax line automatically.

findings.finding: Printify Pop-Up Store: the seller is the Merchant of Record for every sale and is responsible for their own tax obligations. Printify help articles conflict on whether sales tax is added to customers' Pop-Up orders (one says not applied to customers, another says applied by default where applicable).
findings.applyHow: Merch sales run outside Stripe, so Stripe Tax will not count them toward nexus thresholds; add merch revenue by state manually when checking thresholds. In-game merch shop should deep-link out to the Pop-Up Store product page (behind the grown-up gate) so checkout, shipping address and returns stay on Printify's flow and no child-side data is collected by the game.

findings.finding: Stripe's restricted-businesses list restricts 'Sale of in-game currency or game items, unless the business is the operator of the virtual world' (so the game's own operator selling its own gems is the permitted case). It restricts stored value/credits issued by anyone other than the seller. Prohibited: games of chance, sweepstakes/contests with monetary or material prizes, and game tournaments with monetary or material prizes. The page says nothing specific about sales to minors.
findings.applyHow: Gems must be closed-loop: spendable only in this game, never transferable between players, never cashable, never redeemable for merch discounts with cash value issued by a third party. No paid-entry contests or leaderboard events with merch or cash prizes, and no gem-entry raffles for physical merch (that would look like a prohibited sweepstakes/game of chance on Stripe and re-create a loot box). Free giveaways with no purchase are a separate legal question, not covered here.

findings.finding: Stripe US dispute fee: $15 per dispute received, plus $15 if countered (returned if won), per Stripe pricing page as returned by search. Card network programs: Visa VAMP ratio = (disputes + early fraud warnings) / captured payments; 'excessive' merchant threshold is 1.5% outside CEMEA from April 1 2026 with a count of 1,500; Stripe's table also lists a lower 'non-compliant' level of 0.5% with a count of 5, at which Visa 'may' assess fees. Mastercard Excessive Chargeback Merchant: 100-299 chargebacks and 1.5-2.99% rate, fines from month two starting at $1,000. Monitoring programs count disputes regardless of outcome and do not net out refunds. Stripe's dispute-prevention guidance: clear statement descriptor, clear billing terms and agreement click, easy cancel, flexible refund policy, receipts.
findings.applyHow: A $15 fee wipes out a $2-$10 gem pack, so refund generously instead of fighting: publish a plain refund policy ('unused gems refunded within 14 days, kid-bought-by-accident refunds on request') with a refund request link in the game and in every receipt. Use a recognizable statement descriptor that names the game. Always email a Stripe receipt. Add a server-side per-card/per-device daily and monthly spending cap (e.g. a low default the grown-up can raise) to limit 'my kid spent $300' disputes. Do not store cards for one-tap repeat buys: require Checkout each time.

findings.finding: Apple App Review Guidelines (current text): 3.1.1 in-app features such as in-game currencies must use in-app purchase; loot boxes must disclose odds before purchase. 3.1.3(e): physical goods or services consumed outside the app must use purchase methods other than in-app purchase (Apple Pay or card entry). 3.1.1(a): on the United States storefront, apps may include buttons, external links or other calls to action to other purchasing mechanisms without an entitlement; elsewhere that is prohibited without one. 1.3 Kids Category: no links out of the app or purchasing opportunities unless in a designated area behind a parental gate; no third-party analytics/ads (limited exceptions). 5.1.4: the parental gate is not the same as COPPA parental consent.
findings.applyHow: If wrapped for iOS: gems, passes and all digital unlocks must go through Apple in-app purchase, or (US storefront only) an external link to the web Stripe checkout; merch must NOT use in-app purchase and should open the merch site or use card/Apple Pay. Keep the two catalogs cleanly separated in code (digital SKU list vs. physical merch list) so the wrapper can swap the payment path per platform. If listed in the Kids Category, both shop and merch links must sit behind Apple's style of parental gate, which the existing grown-up gate already approximates.

findings.finding: Epic v. Apple status as of late 2026: US-storefront external purchase links allowed since Apple's May 1 2025 guideline change following the contempt ruling. Ninth Circuit (Dec 2025) upheld contempt but sent the case back so the district court can set a permissible commission on linked-out purchases ('reasonably necessary... but no more') and allowed Apple to require equal rather than greater prominence for external links. The Supreme Court granted certiorari June 30 2026 (No. 25-1311), limited to the contempt question; Apple filed its merits brief Sept 14 2026. Per Apple's filing it is currently charging no commission on link-out purchases. A decision is not expected before roughly mid-2027 (secondary estimate). Whether the district-court remand is stayed is unclear from sources.
findings.applyHow: The web/PWA with Stripe is the best-margin path and needs no store approval; keep it primary. An iOS wrapper for US users could link out to the same web checkout at 0% Apple commission today, but that could change after the Supreme Court ruling, so do not price gems on the assumption it stays free. Outside the US an iOS wrapper needs Apple IAP for gems.

findings.finding: Google Play Payments policy: digital goods, in-app features and virtual currency in Play-distributed apps must use Play billing; Play billing must NOT be used for physical goods; randomized items must disclose odds before purchase. US-specific: since Oct 29 2025 (Epic v. Google injunction, upheld by the Ninth Circuit Sept 12 2025) Google does not require Play Billing for US users and does not prohibit links to outside purchases or telling users about other prices. Google's US programs carry service fees with reporting from Oct 1 2026 (download-fee reporting moved to Feb 1 2027). June 24 2026 Android Developers Blog: from June 30 2026 in the US, EEA and UK the service fee starts at 10% on the first $1M of annual earnings and for auto-renewing subscriptions, plus a 5% billing fee only when Google Play Billing is used (not charged on alternative billing or external links). Google and Epic signed a new settlement March 4 2026 and asked the court for a revised injunction; secondary sources conflict on whether it was approved or later withdrawn (one claims withdrawal July 15 2026).
findings.applyHow: If wrapped for Android (e.g. a Trusted Web Activity): gems sold to US users may use the web Stripe checkout via Google's external links/alternative billing programs, but expect roughly a 10% Google service fee and reporting duties on those sales; merch must stay off Play billing. Exact rates and the settlement status were not confirmed from a court source, so re-read the Play Console Help pages before wrapping. An installable PWA from the developer's own site avoids all of this.

findings.finding: State app store accountability laws require app stores to verify age and get parental consent for minors' downloads and in-app purchases, and require developers to act on age signals: Texas SB 2420 took effect after the Fifth Circuit stayed a preliminary injunction (May 28 2026 per secondary source) and emergency relief was denied in July 2026; Texas also requires developers to assign age ratings to apps and in-app purchases. Utah SB 142 developer obligations were due May 6 2026 (current status unclear). Louisiana delayed to July 1 2027. California AB 1043 takes effect Jan 1 2027 (OS-level age-range signals). Alabama Jan 1 2027. These apply to apps distributed through app stores; applicability to a pure web game was not established by the sources.
findings.applyHow: Another reason to stay web-first. If a store wrapper ships later, plan to read the store's age-range signal and disable purchasing entirely for accounts flagged as minors without parental approval, on top of the in-game grown-up gate.

findings.finding: Cross-source pattern: every regulator source reviewed converges on the same short list for games minors play: real-money price visible at the point of spending virtual currency (FTC Genshin order, CPC principle 1, CAP guidance, DFA Art. 14); no paid randomized rewards for minors (FTC Genshin under-16 ban, DFA Art. 15); no time-pressure offers aimed at children (CPC Star Stable action); spending disabled by default with parental unlock (CPC principle 7, DFA recital 62); affirmative consent per charge and no retaliation for disputes (FTC Epic order); no direct exhortation of children to buy (CPC principle 7, CAP Code).
findings.applyHow: Safe new spend types for this game: direct-priced cosmetic items and bundles with fixed, visible contents; permanent expansions (new trail area, new business type) sold for dollars; a non-renewing supporter pass; gem packs matched to item prices; physical merch via outbound link, optionally with a free in-game cosmetic code included with a merch order (a fixed, disclosed bonus, not random). Avoid: countdown or 'today only' offers, limited-stock counters, streak-loss pressure tied to paying, paid speed-ups of timers, random rewards, a second paid currency, and any shop prompt that interrupts play. Shop is entered only from a menu, through the grown-up gate, with a per-device spending cap and an emailed receipt for every purchase.

The 'over 37M notified' figure is from the Sept 2023 claims-process release (emails to more than 37 million people), not from the refund releases. The FTC June 2025 release URL I tried returned 404, so the refund-round figures were confirmed through press coverage quoting the FTC.

Confirmed: Jan 17 2025, $20M, proposed order needing a federal judge's approval. Wording nuances: the release says under-16s need a parent's 'express consent' and that loot boxes must be purchasable with 'real money' (not specifically 'US dollars'); it also requires disclosure of odds AND exchange rates for multi-tier virtual currency, and deletion of under-13 data absent parental consent. The 5-0 vote was to refer the matter to DOJ; BOTH Ferguson and Holyoak concurred on Counts I-II and dissented on Counts III-V. Ferguson's statement: he concurs on the COPPA count and the loot-box-odds deception count and dissents 'as to the rest of the complaint' (three counts).

I also could not confirm court entry of the Cognosphere order. The FTC case page lists only Jan 17 2025 documents (complaint, stipulation, proposed stipulated order) and no entry date; the page itself does not show the court case number (the stipulation PDF shows C.D. Cal. 2:25-cv-447). One secondary site names the judge as Mark C. Scarsi; not verified against the docket. Sub-facts that do check out: Apitor complaint and proposed order announced Sept 3 2025 (third-party SDK collecting children's geolocation on Android); Illuminate Education order proposed Dec 2025 and finalized June 5 2026 (data security, not a game). The claim 'no FTC game-specific IAP/loot box action in 2026' is a negative I could not prove either way.

Dates confirmed (Jan 16 2025, 5-0; FR April 22 2025; effective June 23 2025; compliance April 22 2026 except some safe-harbor provisions with earlier dates). Important limit on the Feb 25 2026 policy statement (2-0 vote): it covers general-audience and mixed-audience operators that collect data solely to determine age, subject to conditions, and does NOT reach services directed to children. It is enforcement discretion only, does not amend the Rule, and does not bind state attorneys general. A game treated as child-directed cannot rely on it.

Confirmed against the FAQ: animated characters are one factor and 'some animated characters are directed to a general audience'; mixed-audience services may age-screen but 'may not block children from participating altogether'; internal-operations support covers maintaining/analysing functioning, authentication, personalization ('game scores, or character choices in virtual worlds') and contextual ads, and 'does not include behavioral advertising'; card consent needs a monetary transaction with 'notification of each discrete transaction to the primary account holder'; 'collecting a 16-digit credit or debit card number alone would not satisfy the method'. Added nuance: a service whose PRIMARY audience is children 'must treat all visitors as children' and generally may not age-screen at all; the age-screen option exists only for mixed-audience services.

Confirmed from a law-firm summary only (statute text not read): effective July 1 2025; express affirmative consent; free-to-paid conversions covered; annual reminder stating renewal frequency, amount and how to cancel; cancellation through the same channel used to subscribe. Core confirmed via secondary sources (the Commission PDF and press release did not render): published 21 March 2025, non-binding, seven principles, covers currency bought with real money, excludes gameplay-only currency and crypto, real-money price display for currency and items, 14-day withdrawal incl. unused currency, protection of children; Star Stable action launched the same day after a Swedish Consumers' Association complaint. I did not verify the exact wording of each of the seven principles (e.g. 'spending disabled by default', 'whales') against the primary text. One sentence is unsupported: the cited 3 June 2025 Commission page does NOT say dialogue was unsatisfactory or mention nine companies; it only describes a stakeholder workshop. The nine-company coordinated CPC action is real but dates from about 15 October 2026 (loot boxes, dark patterns, direct exhortations to children). 'Commission said dialogue was unsatisfactory' is unverified.

Verified against the proposal text: COM(2026) 1100 final, Brussels 11.11.2026, 2026/0356 (COD); a Regulation repealing Directive 2005/29/EC (Art. 38); applies '[12 months after the entry into force]'. Art. 14(1) monetary value of items priced in paid-for virtual currency; Art. 14(2) paid-for virtual currencies disabled by default for minors, activated only on parent/guardian approval (this is in the operative article, not only recital 62); Art. 15 probability disclosure, disable tool for all consumers, no paid variable reward systems for minors; Art. 16 no pay-to-progress/pay-to-win for minors; Art. 17 addictive design off-switches; Art. 20 onward free-trial and renewal reminders. Recital 62 confirms an age rating (trader's own, app-store, PEGI or comparable) indicating suitability for under-18s makes a product 'directed at minors'. Nuances: the 'full price without quantity discounts' and prominence language sits in the recitals, Art. 14(1) itself says 'indicate'; the explanatory memorandum describes Art. 17 as giving the off-switch to 'consumers who are not minors' (minors handled under a separate proposed EU KIDS Act); the drip-pricing prohibition is stated in the explanatory summary, I did not locate the operative article number. Loyalty-programme points are excluded from 'virtual currency'. Proposal only; text may change.

Confirmed from primary PDFs: ASA notice says 'We will begin actively monitoring from 26 May 2026 followed by targeted enforcement action', applies to Apple App Store and Google Play listings, and labels such as 'Offers In-App Purchases' are 'insufficient on their own'. CAP guidance: storefronts using currency that can be earned in-game as well as purchased are 'very unlikely' to be advertising (case-by-case, not an absolute exclusion); storefronts selling currency for real money are in scope; bundle pricing/odd-pricing and direct exhortation to children are covered. Ukie: 11 principles, 18 July 2023, 12-month implementation confirmed. Unverified: the January 2026 government statement (only one low-quality secondary source); the 'ads must not imply paying is the only route' and 'app store listings always in remit' sentences were not located verbatim.

I also found no CMA guidance specific to in-game purchases or virtual currency for 2025-2026. What does exist (secondary sources, not read in full): the DMCC Act unfair commercial practices provisions came into force 6 April 2025; the CMA consulted on price transparency (drip pricing) guidance from 3 July 2025 and published final guidance in November 2025; an older gov.uk 'Principles for online and app-based games' predates the DMCC Act. The source URL attached to this finding is an ASA statement, not a CMA document.

Confirmed on Stripe pages: 'it's up to you to confirm whether registration is actually required'; home US state not monitored; notifications require $10,000 revenue in the previous year; country-only US addresses are 'US unattributed revenue'; Arizona, Indiana, North Carolina count nontaxable sales; Tax Basic 0.5% per transaction (no-code/Checkout) or 50 cents (API), only where registered, registration and filing NOT included; Tax Complete from $90/month on a 1-year contract with registration and filing included. The $90 tier is capped at 2 registrations/yr, 200 transactions/mo, 4 filings/yr; next tier is $430. Washington: $100,000 gross sales, previous or current calendar year. Thresholds: Stripe's guide states $100,000 or 200 transactions for most states and $500,000 for Texas and California; it does not name New York or Alabama. Other sources: New York is $500,000 AND 100 transactions; Alabama $250,000. Several states (incl. California) have dropped transaction-count tests, so '200 transactions' applies to a shrinking set. Monitoring also assumes all sales are taxable at destination.

Oregon DOR: 'Oregon doesn't have a general sales or use/transaction tax.' (A vehicle use tax exists, irrelevant here.) The Stripe Oregon page quote was not fetched; the out-of-state obligation point is consistent with Stripe's monitoring docs, which exclude only the home state.

Confirmed. Restricted: 'Sale of in-game currency or game items, unless the business is the operator of the virtual world' and 'Sale of stored value or credits maintained, accepted, and issued by anyone other than the seller'. Prohibited: 'Games of chance including gambling, internet gambling, casino games, sweepstakes and contests' and 'Games of skill including video game and mobile game tournaments or competitions' with a monetary or material prize. Charity sweepstakes/raffles are a separate restricted category. No mention of minors.

Confirmed: $15.00 per dispute received; $15.00 countered fee, returned for won disputes. VAMP ratio = (disputes + early fraud warnings) / captured payments; excessive threshold 1.5% and count 1,500 outside CEMEA; non-compliant threshold 0.5% and count 5, where Visa 'may assess fees'. Mastercard ECM 100-299 chargebacks and 1.5-2.99%, $1,000 fine in months 2-3. Programs ignore refunds and outcomes. Not found on the page read: the 'from April 1 2026' effective date for the 1.5% threshold (unverified). Extra facts: a transaction appearing as both a fraud warning and a dispute is counted twice; disputes resolved through pre-dispute products are excluded from the VAMP count.

Confirmed against current guideline text: 3.1.1 (in-game currencies must use in-app purchase; loot boxes must disclose odds before purchase; IAP-bought currency may not expire); 3.1.1(a) (US storefront apps may include buttons, external links or other calls to action without entitlements, prohibited in other storefronts); 3.1.3(e) (physical goods must use methods other than in-app purchase, such as Apple Pay or card entry); 1.3 (no links out or purchasing opportunities unless behind a parental gate; no PII or device info to third parties; third-party analytics/ads should not be included, limited exceptions); 5.1.4 (parental gate is generally not the same as parental consent under privacy statutes).
